stories.headline: Judge dismisses Trump's $10 billion suit against the Wall Street Journal over Epstein letter
stories.summary: A federal judge in Miami dismissed President Trump's revised defamation suit against the Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch over a 2025 story about a birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein. The ruling was with prejudice, which bars the same claims from being filed again. Trump has denied writing the letter; whether he will appeal was not reported in the digest.
stories.why_it_matters: The ruling is a test of how hard it is for a public figure to win a libel case over reporting on him, and it ends this attempt to use the courts against a major newspaper.
stories.background: In July 2025 the Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had sent Epstein a letter, with a drawing, for a 2003 birthday book. Trump denied writing it and sued the Journal, its parent company and Murdoch for $10 billion. In April 2026 Judge Darrin Gayles dismissed the first complaint without prejudice and let Trump file an amended one. Public figures must show a publisher acted with actual malice, meaning it knew a statement was false or recklessly disregarded the truth.

facts.text: U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that Trump had not shown the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice.

NPR and ABC report the judge described Trump as 'grasping at straws'.

stories.headline: Judge bars DOJ from threatening election workers; analysis questions its noncitizen list
stories.summary: A federal judge issued a temporary restraining order on Friday blocking the Justice Department from threatening or coercing election workers with prosecution over ballots it says belong to ineligible voters. Separately, an outside analysis found more than 40% of names on a DOJ list of alleged noncitizens in California are not on the state's voter rolls. The midterms are Tuesday.
stories.why_it_matters: The order affects whether local officials can keep counting ballots without fear of federal charges, and the analysis bears on how reliable the government's basis for those demands is.
stories.background: In the weeks before the midterms the Justice Department sent letters to state and local election officials demanding they set aside ballots of voters it flagged as possible noncitizens, and warned of criminal prosecution if they did not. Election officials challenged those demands in court. The department's list of flagged names had not been independently checked until this analysis. Noncitizens are barred from voting in federal elections.

facts.text: A federal judge on Friday issued a temporary restraining order barring the administration from threatening election workers with criminal prosecution for counting ballots from voters it claims are ineligible.
The order says officials cannot be forced to separate out or stop counting ballots the government deems disputed.

An outside analysis found more than 40% of names on the DOJ list of alleged noncitizens in California are not on the state's voter rolls and that thousands of citizens appear to be flagged.

stories.headline: FBI blames North Korea for record $6.3 billion Binance hack
stories.summary: The FBI said on Saturday that North Korea-linked hackers were behind this week's theft from the crypto exchange Binance, reported as about $6.3 billion. Binance said it has replaced most of the lost funds and began resuming withdrawals on Sunday. Exchanges are reported to be tightening security.
stories.why_it_matters: Customers of crypto exchanges are exposed to the security of those platforms, and a theft of this size raises questions about how safe held assets are. State-linked theft also funds sanctioned governments.
stories.background: Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange. The FBI tied the theft to "malicious cyber activity" by a group it calls TraderTraitor, which it also linked to last year's $1.5 billion Bybit hack. North Korea has been repeatedly accused of stealing crypto to fund its government. Binance suspended withdrawals after the attack and has pledged to reimburse customers in full.

facts.text: The FBI said the attack was tied to North Korean activity by a group known as TraderTraitor.
The stolen amount was reported as about $6.3 billion, described as the largest crypto theft on record.

TraderTraitor is the same group the FBI blamed for a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year.

stories.headline: Binance loses about $6 billion in crypto theft, says it will cover losses
stories.summary: Hackers took roughly $6 billion to $6.3 billion in digital assets from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, in what outlets describe as the biggest crypto heist on record. Binance halted withdrawals and said it is working to recover funds and will cover the losses. Some analysts point to North Korea.
stories.why_it_matters: People who hold crypto on exchanges are exposed to the exchange's security and solvency. A loss this size at the largest platform is likely to shake confidence in the sector and crypto prices.
stories.background: Binance is the largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume and holds customer assets on its platform. Exchanges are frequent hacking targets, and North Korea-linked groups have been blamed for earlier large thefts. Binance has previously used an emergency fund to repay users after smaller incidents. This theft is reported to be far larger than earlier record heists. Binance's founder posted updates publicly while the company worked to respond.

facts.text: Binance halted withdrawals after hackers took about $6 billion in assets, PBS NewsHour reported.

Binance said it will cover the losses, according to The New York Times.
NPR also put the theft at $6.3 billion and linked it to North Korea in its explainer.

stories.headline: OPEC+ set to keep December oil output targets unchanged
stories.summary: Reuters and Bloomberg, citing sources and delegates, report that major OPEC+ producers will keep oil production targets steady in December. Bloomberg said the Middle East conflict continues to curb part of the group's output. No official statement was found at the time of writing.
stories.why_it_matters: Steady quotas mean no new supply from the group, which matters for fuel prices at the pump while the Iran war disrupts Gulf production.
stories.background: OPEC+ is the alliance of OPEC members and allies led by Saudi Arabia and Russia that sets oil output targets. It finished unwinding a large batch of earlier supply cuts in September and has held targets since. The war involving Iran has pushed some Gulf producers below their quotas. The group is also reviewing members' capacity ahead of setting 2027 baselines, per reports.

facts.text: OPEC+ agreed in principle to keep December oil output targets steady, Reuters reported citing sources.
Two delegates told Bloomberg the group is set to stick with unchanged quotas, with Middle East conflict curbing part of its output.

stories.headline: Oil companies report another quarter of high profits as war lifts fuel prices
stories.summary: NPR and CNBC report that oil companies posted strong quarterly earnings, with refining profits rising as fuel supplies tightened during the Iran war. CNBC notes this follows President Trump's criticism that the companies made too much money. The Financial Times reports the major companies are resisting pressure to build new refineries.
stories.why_it_matters: High refining margins feed into gasoline and diesel prices that drivers and businesses pay.
stories.background: The war involving Iran has pushed up oil prices and disrupted fuel supply. Conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine have also cut refining capacity, according to the FT. Refiners earn the margin between crude and the fuel they sell, so tight supply raises that margin. Politicians in both parties have criticized industry profits.

facts.text: NPR reported oil companies posted another quarter of very high profits as the Iran war lifted oil and pump prices.
CNBC reported refining earnings of oil majors have surged since Trump said they made too much money.
The Financial Times reported oil majors are resisting pressure to invest in new refineries even as fuel prices rise.

stories.headline: Four dead after e-bike battery fire in a Bronx apartment
stories.summary: A fire that started with an e-bike battery inside a Mott Haven apartment on Wednesday has now killed four people, including a boy and two teenagers, according to the NYPD. The FDNY says e-bike fires have risen sharply across the city. The family's neighbors are mourning while officials point to the rise in battery fires.
stories.why_it_matters: Lithium-ion e-bike batteries charged or stored indoors, and bikes left near an exit, are a danger to anyone living in a city apartment building.
stories.background: Lithium-ion batteries power most e-bikes and scooters, and they can ignite quickly if damaged or overheated. The FDNY has tracked a rise in battery fires in recent years. This fire broke out early on Wednesday, Oct. 28, in a Patterson Houses apartment in Mott Haven, a public housing complex in the Bronx. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said officials had identified an e-bike battery as the cause, and Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said the bike was in the pathway of the exit door.

facts.text: Two teenage boys, aged 16 and 15, and a 33-year-old woman have died along with Zion Maine, the NYPD said, bringing the toll to four.
The New York Times reports that the family's apartment fire began with an electric-bike battery on Wednesday.
The FDNY says e-bike fires have risen sharply across New York City.
Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said crews arrived within four minutes and that the e-bike was in the pathway of the exit door; Mayor Mamdani said the cause was an e-bike lithium-ion battery.

stories.headline: Mamdani moves to replace head of Racial Equity Commission
stories.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani sought to remove Linda Tigani as head of the city's Racial Equity Commission after she clashed with his administration, the New York Times reports. Reports say Tigani will stay on for now, and Council members have backed her. The dispute has led some to question the mayor's commitment to reparations.
stories.why_it_matters: The commission is the city body charged with studying racial disparities, including the question of reparations, so who leads it shapes what the city studies and recommends.
stories.background: The Commission on Racial Equity, known as CORE, was created under the City Charter to push the city to address racial disparities. Mamdani, who took office this year, has said he is open to reparations if the commission recommends them. Tigani had criticized a draft racial equity plan, saying it lacked elements the Charter requires. City & State reports Mamdani named NAACP New York leader Christopher Alexander as the new chair. Changing the chair needs approval from the mayor and Council Speaker Julie Menin.

facts.text: Mayor Mamdani sought to remove the head of the Racial Equity Commission, and some have raised questions about his commitment to reparations, the New York Times reports.
City & State reported that City Council members backed Linda Tigani amid Mamdani's plans to replace her.
TheGrio reported Mamdani picked NAACP New York leader Christopher Alexander to chair the commission.

framing.note: Frames the removal as a test of the mayor's reparations commitment.

stories.social: A petition circulated online urging that Tigani be kept as chair and executive director.
